name: Hydrogen peroxide eye drops

lead: Some people have tried putting hydrogen peroxide solution in the eyes hoping to whiten or clean them. It is a household antiseptic, not an ophthalmic product.

Hydrogen peroxide is an oxidising disinfectant that breaks down into water and oxygen. Contact lens systems use 3 percent peroxide with a catalytic disc that neutralises it before lenses go back in the eye. No studies support direct eye use for appearance.

paras: People who try it dilute household peroxide and drop it in the eye hoping for a cleansing effect. Contact lens peroxide systems, which are designed to be neutralised before use, are a separate product.

Reference sources state that concentrations as low as 3% can be dangerous to the eye because oxygen is released inside it. Direct eye use is associated with corneal injury. Higher concentrations cause skin burns and react violently with organic material.

angle.text: Users apply peroxide to the eye hoping it cleanses and whitens. The idea rests on anecdote, and reference sources warn that even 3 percent solution can be dangerous for the eye.

lead: Hydrogen peroxide eye drops refers to putting hydrogen peroxide solution directly into the eye with the aim of whitening or cleansing it, so that the sclera (the white of the eye) looks brighter and less red. Clear, white eyes are part of a rested, healthy appearance, and the idea behind the practice is that peroxide, which is known as a bleaching and antiseptic agent for hair, teeth and surfaces, could do the same for the eye [1]. It is a home or do-it-yourself practice rather than an ophthalmic product, and no published studies of it for appearance were found.

Consumer hydrogen peroxide is usually sold at 3 or 6 percent, laboratories commonly use 30 percent, and industrial grades are much stronger [1]. It is used as an antiseptic, for tooth whitening and, mixed with other agents, in hair colouring, where it gave rise to the phrase 'peroxide blonde' [1]. In the eye-care world, 3 percent peroxide is used to disinfect contact lenses in a case containing a catalytic disc that neutralises it before the lenses are put back in the eye [1][2].

Reference sources caution about eye contact. Wikipedia states that concentrations as low as 3 percent can be dangerous to the eye because oxygen is released within it [1]. An ophthalmologist answering a question for the American Academy of Ophthalmology says 3 percent peroxide rarely causes permanent or severe eye damage, with injury usually confined to the cornea, producing stinging, pain, redness, tearing, and possibly corneal abrasions or ulcers that can be serious if not treated [3].

paras: Hydrogen peroxide was first made in about 1818 by Louis Jacques Thenard, who called it 'eau oxygenee' [1]. Consumers usually buy 3 or 6 percent solutions from pharmacies, laboratories use 30 percent, and industrial grades run from 70 to 98 percent, with solutions above 68 percent able to turn entirely to steam and oxygen [1]. Concentrations up to 35 percent cause white oxygen bubbles and pain on skin [1].
The US Food and Drug Administration generally recognises peroxide as safe as an antimicrobial agent, and pharmaceutical formulations typically come in brown bottles that block light [1].

Three percent peroxide is a common contact lens disinfectant. The lens case contains a catalytic disc that neutralises the peroxide, and the solution and lenses must stay in the case for at least six hours before use [1][2]. Health Canada's alert pages describe consumers who reported pain and burning after the unneutralised solution touched the eye, including a corneal burn confirmed by an eye doctor, in cases where people used a flat case or rinsed lenses with unneutralised solution [2].

Wikipedia states that concentrations as low as 3 percent can be dangerous to the eye because oxygen evolves within it, and that domestic-strength solutions can irritate the eyes and mucous membranes [1]. According to the American Academy of Ophthalmology Q&A, 3 percent peroxide rarely causes permanent or severe damage; injury is usually confined to the cornea, with stinging, pain, redness, tearing, abrasions and ulcers, and the response advises flushing with water immediately and seeing an ophthalmologist [3].
No studies found on hydrogen peroxide drops for eye whitening or appearance.
